name: Hair botox / hair filler treatment

image.caption: Feeling like Samantha after her Botox session. Got a rash after getting facial hair pulled out at the barber shop. :/

lead: Hair botox, or hair filler, is sold to make dry, frizzy or damaged hair look smoother and shinier. Despite the name it is not an injection; the label is a marketing nickname with no standard formula.

It belongs to the family of keratin and Brazilian smoothing treatments, which last roughly two to six months. Marketing says products deposit protein or conditioning agents on the hair fibre to fill rough areas, often followed by heat styling; hair is dead tissue, so they coat the fibre rather than repair it. No trials of products sold under this name were found.

paras: Used in salons and at home as a smoothing step, usually with a flat iron to set the product. Check the ingredient list, since it determines what results and safety information apply.

Safety depends on the actual ingredients. Related smoothing treatments that contain or release formaldehyde have prompted warnings from the FDA, Health Canada and OSHA, and reported effects include eye and respiratory irritation. Regulation differs by country.

angle.text: Hair botox is a marketing name for smoothing treatments that coat the hair to cut frizz and add shine. The look is cosmetic and visible after application. The term has no fixed formula, so results depend on the product.

lead: Hair botox, also marketed as a hair filler treatment, is the name given in the beauty industry to salon and at-home smoothing treatments that are described as depositing protein or conditioning agents on the hair to reduce frizz and add shine. The name borrows from injectable cosmetic procedures; it is a marketing term and has no single standard formulation.

The treatment sits in the same product family as keratin and Brazilian smoothing treatments, which use a smoothing solution sealed into the hair with a flat iron. Encyclopedic sources describe that family as lasting roughly two to six months [1][2]. Some products in the wider family have drawn regulatory attention because of formaldehyde or formaldehyde-releasing ingredients [2], so the ingredient list of an individual hair botox product determines which safety information applies.

No published clinical trials of products sold specifically as hair botox or hair filler treatments were identified. Evidence about the category is limited to descriptions of related smoothing treatments and regulatory records.
infobox: Weeks to months (related keratin treatments: about 2-6 months)[1]
Cosmetic; varies by country and by ingredients

paras: Products sold as hair botox or hair filler are presented as treatments for dry, frizzy, chemically processed or heat-damaged hair. Marketing describes them as filling in rough or damaged areas of the hair fibre with protein or conditioning ingredients, leaving the hair smoother and shinier. Hair is made of dead cells, and encyclopedic sources note that damage to the visible shaft cannot be repaired biologically, so cosmetic products work by coating or depositing material on the fibre [3][4].
The name does not mean the products contain botulinum toxin, which is an injectable drug; it is used as a brand-style label for the idea of a smoothing, rejuvenating hair treatment.

Keratin treatments apply a keratin-containing solution to the hair and then seal it with a hot flat iron. Wikipedia describes the results as reduced frizz, straighter hair and added shine, lasting about six months, with the aftercare advice of avoiding washing and tying hair for about three days [1].

Brazilian hair straightening is a related semi-permanent method in which a solution containing formaldehyde or a formaldehyde derivative is sealed in with a flat iron; the effect usually lasts about three months [2]. Wikipedia notes that this method goes by many brand and generic names and is sometimes confused with keratin treatment [2].

Safety concerns in this product family centre on formaldehyde. Wikipedia reports that formaldehyde is classified as a known human carcinogen by IARC (2006) and the US National Toxicology Program, and that reported effects of exposure include eye irritation, respiratory problems, headache, nausea and rash [2]. Air testing in salons has found formaldehyde during smoothing treatments, with a 2011 study reporting levels above OSHA's 15-minute short-term limit during blow drying and an Oregon OSHA study reporting 8-hour averages below the permissible limit [2].

Regulators have acted on specific products: Health Canada issued an advisory in 2010, Oregon OSHA issued warnings in 2010, the US FDA sent a warning letter in 2011 about a manufacturer's 'formaldehyde-free' claims, and a 2012 California settlement required corrected labels and fines [2]. The European Union restricts formaldehyde-releasing cosmetics [2]. Wikipedia describes the keratin treatment as emitting gases and as not recommended during pregnancy, with skin and eye protection required [1].

No studies found. No published human trials of products marketed as hair botox or hair filler treatments were located; the safety literature discussed above concerns related formaldehyde-based smoothing treatments and salon air quality [2].
